Papal Authority. The spiritual and temporal power claimed by the Pope as the head of the Roman Catholic Church and, in medieval Europe, as a political actor wielding influence over emperors, kings, and states. The nature and extent of papal power shifted dramatically across history, particularly during the medieval period when popes crowned emperors and claimed supremacy over secular rulers, and later when ecclesiastical authority was challenged by the Reformation and nation-states.

The papacy's authority derives from Catholic doctrine that Saint Peter, the first Pope, was given by Christ supreme authority over the Church. This spiritual claim became intertwined with medieval claims to temporal, or political, power over European rulers. Medieval popes issued excommunications, spiritual censure, and interdicts, prohibition of church sacraments to entire regions, as political weapons. These measures were genuinely feared by Christian rulers because they affected salvation and popular legitimacy.

The Investiture Controversy from ten seventy-six to eleven twenty-two was the defining medieval conflict over papal authority: could emperors appoint bishops, which gave them church revenues and political allies, or was that the Pope's exclusive right? The Concordat of Worms in eleven twenty-two affirmed papal rights. The papacy's temporal power in Italy—the Papal States—gave popes actual armies and territory. This necessitated popes function as political rulers, sometimes corrupting ecclesiastical integrity with dynastic ambitions and secular warfare.

The Reformation beginning in fifteen seventeen challenged papal authority directly. Protestant theologians denied papal infallibility and the Pope's exclusive authority to interpret scripture. Martin Luther rejected the Pope's authority over Christian conscience. The Council of Trent from fifteen forty-five to fifteen sixty-three and the Counter-Reformation reasserted papal authority within Catholicism but with a weakened claim to universal dominion. Nation-states increasingly asserted sovereignty over their own churches and religious affairs. It connects to Christianity, the religion that centers on the Pope's authority, to the Holy Roman Empire, the political system in which papal authority was contested with secular power, to Medieval Europe, the era when papal authority reached its peak, and to the Reformation, the movement that challenged papal authority fundamentally.
